comment_text.value:
I think a chatbot or voice is a horrible interface for most things. There is 0 chance for discoverability, so the application's function is limited by the user's imagination. Most people aren't going to think about the various things a program could solve for them. Even with a UI, most users only use a small fraction of the available options. Without some visual cue to let them know features exist, I'd bet that most users would use even less.

My day job is automation stuff within a large organization. Most people, even within a technical organization, don't seem to think about how the computer can solve problems for them. The other day I used Claude to turn a massive csv dump of data into a dashboard to see trends over time. I don't see other people doing that.. but if Excel had a button for it, I'm sure they would do it.

comment_text.value:
It’s interesting that Boris Tadić, the former president of Serbia (part of the previous regime, who lost to Vučić 14 years ago) echoes the same type of pronouncements about politicians and the commenters here on HN, and I do not mean this in a particularly laudatory sense. Just recently he was sending messages about how political experience, political vision and the like are key. How to be a political leader one needs this or that, or how Serbia requires this or that type of engagement with future technologies to remain relevant, comparing the student movement to blockchain (yes, really). This (incredibly vain and pompous) man doubtlessly has the most political experience in Serbia right now, and sits in several boards of Chinese and other multinationals, with other consulting roles, pretty much proving the bankability of his political talents. And yet that’s the person behind a series of political decisions and circumstances which inaugurated the previous regime.

Also, looking around the globe at professional politicians once also lauded for their political talent, like Macron, or Merkel, I’m really not seeing their policies paying off in spades, nor their "political vision" proving particularly beneficial to their citizenry at the moment. In all three cases, it seems, seasoned politicians made capital errors in judgement which are now causing resentment, almost unprecedented political realignments and upheaval across these nations. People are incredibly quick to judge the potential behaviour of a future political formation - yet Western democracies are by and large falling apart, as a result of career politicians’ actions, inactions, stupidity and avarice? As people speak more and more loudly on certain issues, like Palestine, these same politicians are comfortable ignoring them. Where is the scepticism for them, or the viability of this guild-like way of structuring the political sphere as the way forward? We are living the consequences of having career politicians lead, do we like it so much we cannot conceive of anything better?

Anyway, if you look into the local press in Serbia and especially enclaves like Twitter, there’s a wonderful symmetry: the EU champions are terrified the student movement has already shown "concerning" right leanings, they’re busy counting how many EU flags the students have draped themselves in while marching, and aren’t happy. The right is deeply worried about how the "globalist, NGO, pro-EU camarilla" is already deeply embedded in the student movement (they went to Brussels, after all!) and is perhaps even planting their candidates into the mix to sell out the country’s interests to the globalists. I am being slightly ironic here, but I have nothing but contempt for this thinking on both sides. Winning the election required the participation and support from both these camps’ voting blocks, which tells you how bad the situation truly was, since sworn enemies were forced to cooperate with a political unknown just for the chance to win against the existing political regime.

In a sense, only a political unknown could have won, as all pre-existing political factions, (mostly comprised of these praised seasoned politicians, many of them three decades into their careers) would not or could not muster the strength or wherewithal to work with one another. No nationalist would ever cooperate with a globalist pro-EU green party, even if it cost them their country, democracy, and those same national interests they hold sacrosanct. Likewise, no progressive citizen party saving democratic principles would ever work with what they view as backward retrograde nationalist movements threatening to plunge the country back into the type of rhetoric and milieu as existed during the wars of the nineties. Also, at some point the decades-long careers of many politicians was perfect cannon fodder for the regime’s propaganda machine, gleefully cataloguing their past sins and outright inventing them if the need arose. After a while, political experience morphs into evidence of one’s political parasitism.

It took a decentralised student movement which could not be targeted and besmirched, to engage the non-voting public and voters on both sides of the political spectrum. Part of the reason why all parties which took part in this election were swept away (except for the students and the outgoing regime) was because of failing to recognise the political moment. This election, in my view, was a single-issue election - the workings of democracy and stopping corruption and the further decay of institutions. This is what the political movement will be judged on, and what will determine its political future. The citizenry, at this juncture, is willing to table discussions on foreign policy for the sake of internal affairs and weeding out corruption. Most foreign powers and press corps, sadly, are interested primarily in the foreign policy implications of this new movement, and seem like they couldn’t care less if Serbian citizenry lives in caves, favelas, or in a thriving democracy.

Many things are still unclear, such as the exact relationship between the Parliament and Government, once formed, and the direct democracy practiced by the student movement. It is unclear how effective it will prove, or how they will select their allies and collaborators, as it’s perfectly obvious that the movement cannot simply replace the totality of public administration. Regardless, the new regime will enjoy a broad latitude and a measure of good will among the citizenry not seen in a generation. It needs to use that to good effect. If it fails to deliver, they will be ridiculed and attacked by members of both internal factions, and will more than likely splinter, and usher in a return of Vučić, who - lest we forget - is now the only opposition party in Parliament, with a sizeable number of representatives, and plenty of corrosive residuals and slush funds and media operations still at his disposal. Lest we also forget, with 700k party members, it is a powerful organisation even without the corruptive backend of the state apparatus.

comment_text.value:
Strings are trivial in C++. Drawing 2D graphics is fine, many libraries do it. Creating old-fashioned component frameworks (like Qt, JUCE, etc) is easy. I implemented all those things on my own, decades before AI.

The hard bit is when you have complex, responsive layouts involving text. (And styling it)

Something seemingly trivial like an agent-style chat containing markdown text blocks, where it's expandable and smoothly scrollable is insanely difficult. The only frameworks that do this well are browsers, and the amount of horrible, horrible logic hidden inside them to make it look easy is hard to believe.

And since in many agents you're also going to want to display actual HTML, unless you're going to embed a browser engine in your C++ library, that's just not doable.

comment_text.value:
Nice to see a gui coding agent. I use tui agents all the time but I am building a gui one. I use Claude Code, Codex, opencode and a couple other but I do not like the DX/UX.

I often want click a part of the wall of text (from agent) and search for related text, open them up on the side or so. I want to open a linked file. I want to answer multiple questions in an async manner, even come back and continue answering the next day.

There are many prompt level features I want too - orchestrate with subagents, but only the tasks I select - how do I select when there is no checkbox. Or maybe delegate a subagent to dig into (read only) one portion of the chat response. Maybe codify (write) only one task in a list of tasks. So many many other small things.

As a full-time user of coding agents, the TUI barely works for me. I think splitting text, searching in text, merging text are more important in agent driven development than ever before. It is all text, all the way. This is what I am building myself, with my own gui framework.

Paseo is Apache 2.0 (vs T3 MIT). Haven't tried T3 and can't find docs for it to get more insight without installing.

Re: changes: Paseo's plugin system is very, very good. Some limitations since not all of the internals are accessible via plugin system, but allows building very custom UIs. So this may be a point of delta with T3. But I have some coworkers that have gone absolutely HAM with the plugins and built entirely custom workspaces (wild).

For me, what I have found most useful about Paseo is the multi-platform, multi-agent setup because this has given my agent teams much, much more autonomy that I feel like I can trust (after weeks of watching them work). The agent profile system looks too simple at first blush, but actually, that simplicity and semi-structured dynamic nature of the sub-agents is what makes it powerful.

Might try T3 for a week and see; thanks for sharing!

EDIT: T3 has no docs site yet, but sifting through docs, this was interesting: https://github.com/pingdotgg/t3code/blob/main/docs/user/remo...

“Traditionally, a lot of these decisions flow through engineering managers, PMs, and designers. That becomes increasingly difficult as engineers get faster.

How do you organize a team where engineers can build much faster, without creating bottlenecks around decisions and reviews?

Our bet is to push more ownership to engineers. Rather than adding more layers of management, we want engineers to handle more of the planning, execution, and review themselves.”

My bet was to push more ownership to the PMs and designers.

Engineering’s job is now to make that process sustainable and tackle the items that aren’t directly visible but still matter.

I find it interesting that they’ve opened up PRs to the org, but didn’t land on using the review process to refine a system that guides AI toward writing better and better code. I’m a graybearded “wizard” who is highly technical, and that’s where I landed.

We’ve had a very similar arc, but I’m at the point where I would be more likely to hire an artist for a frontend design position than an engineer:

“Use AI to make the app beautiful. You report to product.”

Engineers are checking the code and fixing architectural and abstraction issues behind the scenes. We’re making tests that keep AI from making the same mistake twice. We’re also figuring out how to run tests at unprecedented scale without slowing these non-technical “devs” down. There are plenty of technical challenges scaling this path that need the traditional engineering brain and a deep knowledge of development. It’s not just 20x productivity, it’s a lot of fun. I’m buried in new and interesting technical challenges these days.

We gave our old Legos to the others, now we’re having fun with our new Legos.

I think my English is a bit lacking, so I didn't explain my situation well enough.

The main point is not that everything is solved if you specify all the conjunction conditions and prove that those conjunction conditions are correct. Rather, the key point is that in that process, the agent keeps expanding subgoals.

It goes on like that.

comment_text.value:
While learning and applying formal verification in the context of using AI agents, what I feel is that sometimes it's hard to express my own thoughts as formal verification. But more than that, I doubt whether formal verification being done correctly actually solves the phenomenon of AI spinning in circles on a specific task.

For example, I want to eat chicken, so I try formally verifying "chicken dish," and every time GPT or Claude starts digging into the origin of the sauce in the chicken dish or the breed of the chicken. Then the chicken dish never gets finished and never makes it to dinner, and instead I gain deep knowledge about the origin of chickens.

Of course, I know that formal verification has liveness — meaning that there must be progress in the work is also part of formal verification — but the AI judges that learning the origin of the chicken counts as progress too. Yet it ends up doing work that it actually shouldn't be doing.

Personally, while organizing these AI anti-patterns, I feel that when you formally verify one condition, verification of another condition gets weakened, and within that phenomenon I sense the AI spinning in circles again. In the end, I end up going through the process of reading and merging everything one by one myself, and I want to know whether this is something only I experience.

I think a lot of companies are struggling to move beyond this being a thing developers use to something everyone can use. Developers have to go really far out of their way to build agents and tools that apply the capabilities to their specific business. comment_text.value:
I write a spec by speaking, not much thought given to grammar and sentence structure. I over-describe concepts, over-describe functionality. A lot of repetition of details and concepts. The audience is not a human. Whisper converts it to text.

Lightly manually edit for speech rec failures.

LLM takes that and converts it into a much much denser, much more structured technical spec in markdown. This is issue 1 in the repo.

I edit this directly extensively, adding detail, removing misconceptions, adding sections with more dictated text.

LLM takes this and further densifies it, closer to an actual implementor’s spec. I carefully note what got added, removed, edited in this step.

I edit this carefully and extensively again. Some removals get added back, some additions get removed. This is the first commit and closes issue 1.

I then have an LLM write an implementation plan and basic project scaffolding. Makefiles, smoke tests, logging, test framework, DI. I edit the plan, and the plan is the second commit. An LLM uses both plus scaffolding plus my repo policy documents (global) to write a README. We’re still single threaded.

An agent files the first n top level implementation tickets. These refer to and sometimes quote any interface contracts in the spec or implementation plan. These usually map 1-to-1 to a module/directory. These sometimes have stub commits to create the module directory and commit interface definitions. Some larger modules have a README in their module directory if their purpose or structure or inputs or outputs are complicated or non-obvious.

Parallel agents write commit level issues that are the task items for each top level implementation ticket. One agent per module.

Then, spawn parallel agents with detailed global instructions, the full spec+plan, and the full readme, and the full code from the module it is working in, plus the issue text. Its output is a single commit on the feature branch and a PR that closes out one feature ticket.

This spawns an adversarial reviewer which has detailed agent instructions as well as our code style guides and repo policies. The scaffolding includes tests and linting and checks. Any failures spawn rework agents until the feature branch is up to snuff.

I review the feature branch diff and merge it, having read the review and rework comments on the PR. I frequently add comments about the implementation (“don’t do x, do y”) and add WIP: back to loop it back for more rework. I don’t see anything that isn’t green, formatted, passes linting, passes tests, and a (dumb) bot thinks is ready to land. Most of the time, it is. Sometimes, it did it the wrong way and I correct it.

The more modular the code, the easier it is to parallelize (obviously). It is ridiculously easy to build large software quickly now, provided it is sufficiently modular so the implementation doesn’t have to cross modules very much. The detailed spec and implementation plan up front helps a lot with this. It’s a lot like writing multithreaded programs really.

Any bugs discovered are tackled with strict TDD, one commit with a failing test, one bugfix commit that must be green and not touch the test.

Individual modules must conform to good contracts, meet best OOP practices, and fit into context. Too big and they get broken down further. Context size is actually a useful constraint for code structure here.

This workflow, the code standards, the styleguide, the linter settings, the fmt settings (obviously only applicable to non-Go as the Go fmt is not configurable), everything is global and stored in another repo and is vendored into each AI managed project repo. It has a fair bit of “I shouldn’t have to say this, but…” stuff (in the style of “fire codes are written in blood” - each warning sign came from experience).

My results are quite good. It’s as the saying goes, much like managing a team of junior devs. It is easy to end up with a LOT of parallel implementors, reviewers, reworkers, and tons of CI, but it’s still so much vastly cheaper than humans that it doesn’t matter.

Someone will make a LOT of money wringing out the inefficiencies from this workflow, because I think the “agent as replacement for third-world contracted junior dev” model is the one almost everyone is using right now.

comment_text.value:
If it's not obvious from the title, I'm a VC and I spend a ton of time in meetings with founders. What's less obvious is all the other things. After treading water for at least a decade, I am deeply suspect of any VC's organizational capabilities. Mostly my own.

Believe it or not, for the longest time, my notes lived in saved (and unsaved) text files in Sublime Text. At some point I've tried using TiddlyWiki, bandwagoned onto Notion and Obsidian, and once even opened Microsoft OneNote. My brain doesn't work like that, the 5,715 unread emails in my inbox is proof of a losing battle.

Asana helped, I tried sprint planning like my time working for a startup, but I quickly learned you can’t budget 10 points for firefighting. A more recent addition has been Granola, great UI, but I realize I actually don't find AI notetakers helpful. If you can imagine, I look at 2,000 companies a year, and meet just under a quarter of them, at some point they all start to blend together.

Logseq came the closest, the daily journal clicked for me, but I wanted mobile, reliable sync, and a search that didn’t need the gentle touch of a crowbar. I love you Logseq team. <3

So I built a tool of my own, DayCarp (daycarp.com) it’s a minimalist notetaker with Sublime’s minimap, Granola’s AI notetaking, Logseq’s journal, and some of Asana’s tasking. It also has nice quality of life features like inline images, templates, Excel-style calculations when you highlight numbers, and of course AI, bring your own API key, self-host, or use mine.

Go to DayCarp.com and try it free, would appreciate the roast. It’s something I genuinely use every day, and I think others might find useful.

Here’s how I take notes in a meeting with a founder:

1. I setup my framework with these headings: Team, Product, Business Model, IP/Regulatory, Market, Competition, Traction, Financing, Decision & Next Steps. This is my mental framework, and also roughly the order by which I ask questions. I start with getting to know the people, and end with the financing discussion. It’s not unlike a sales call from the VC side as well, we need to sell great founders as much as founders need great VCs.

2. Under each heading I put a bullet or two about things I learned about the company after spending all of 45 seconds looking at their deck or website. I usually also put one or two things in common with the founder that I can bring up in conversation.

3. I put “Q: [question]”; under each bullet where I want to push the founder, for tech-heavy pre-revenue startups I might push on IP, or problem; for a classic SaaS, I’ll try to push on quality of traction. I’ll also try to size the market to get an idea, founders often share a massive number in an unrelated market.

4. If I don’t have much time, I’ll pitch the startup back to the founder “I understand you do XYZ for so and so, did I understand that correctly?”, that saves about 10 minutes off the pitch. I’ll also preface that I’m conversational and that we might jump around, to avoid the pitch entirely. Totally. Better solutions come through those explainer sessions.

I feel like this is quite a different situation. Building a nuclear weapon requires a lot of things to happen in the physical world that we can watch for. Weapons grade fissile materials must be sourced or refined, facilities must be build, you can't just do this in any machine shop. Various experts must be either poached or subverted or home grown. There are a lot of people with mouths involved. Then once you get past all of that you either have to test or just hope for the best at which point you will certainly be detected and likely handled with extreme prejudice.

Digital intelligence seems much less controllable. Near frontier weights are already out there, you don't necessarily need massive datacenters if you're not trying to serve commercially. Even if we we're somehow able to control what OTHER nations do through either treaties or threats of sanctions/force, working on this stuff is easily in range of many of the larger criminal orgs. Beyond all of that, there's always the chance that weights from authorized providers find their way "out the back door".

We've seen with crypto and darknet markets that even if you can fight this kind of stuff and catch bad actors, the most actual change you're going to effect is a temporary slowdown and the next guy who tries is going to be that much better. I don't doubt that regulation is going to be the initial route this goes, mostly due to the financial interests of the frontier companies and the desire to keep this build-out solvent for as long as possible rather than any true concern for actual safety and sanity. What's really going to need to happen though, in my very insignificant opinion of course, is we are going to have to change from the ground up how our digital infrastructure is built.

Maybe with the coming changes that is for the best too, our current systems are designed for people and I don't know the current numbers but it seems like agent traffic is already the bigger percentage. We may not be able to build our infrastructure on top of these large mountains of human designed legacy code. Maybe we need to be thinking about new kernels, new servers, new protocols and stacks.

We seem to be very quickly reaching a point where is something is not mathematically provable to be secure then it is not secure at all.

comment_text.value:
I genuinely prefer OpenAI models for coding and building in general. My observation: GPT models are generally better at following the system prompt, tool use, and skill use.

I use Paseo and there is a noticeable difference when GPT-6.1 Sol is driving the orchestrator vs Opus/Sonnet 5.5 driving the orchestrator. Anthropic models ignore the shared system prompt to use the Paseo tools for sub-agents and prefer to use its own native sub-agents. It ignores the skills mentioned in the system prompt, but will use them if I explicitly tell it to in a user prompt or I extra emphasize the instruction in an XML fenced block in the system prompt or CLAUDE.md like <BOOTSTRAP_MUST_EXECUTE_AT_START>

Sometimes, I feel like I have to explicitly prompt Anthropic models to behave the way I want it to (even with system prompts in place with the EXACT instruction). Sometimes it even feels like it's disregarding CLAUDE.md. To me, this makes me feel like it is the less compliant of the two because I constantly have to steer it manually. Anthropic models also feels like they prefer to go lone-wolf. I want my orchestrator to use the other subs (configured with different platforms and models) to evaluate a design; Opus really wants to lone-wolf and solo everything.

That said, I prefer Anthropic models generally only when the task is more open ended and exploratory. The Anthropic models' "mind of their own" benefits here; GPT models tend to be too agreeable; and too eager to agree with any change in direction. But for actual coding once a direction/plan is in place, I would much rather delegate it to GPT (more likely to draw on the harness for context, skills, instructions, and tools -> more consistency).

Anthropic's 1m context window default and shorter cache TTL are also not great in agentic flows where an agent could become idle and then re-activated. Burns tokens very quickly. I have it tuned down to 300k across all models (recommend doing this for multi-agent coding).
